There are four primary ways to reduce peaking events in HVAC systems: • Increase system efficiency. This approach will reduce the load whenever the system is running. For specific regions with high humidity loads, a system that provides separate sensible cooling and dehumidification can significantly increase efficiency (Blue Frontier, n.d.; Copeland, n.d.; Mojave Energy Systems, n.d.). • Improve the building envelope, thereby reducing the heat gains and losses as well as reducing the infiltration of outside air. This reduces the overall thermal load the HVAC system needs to condition, thereby reducing its power consumption (Harris 2021; Wijesuriya et al. 2023). 10 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. • Add energy storage systems. This approach will store energy during off-peak periods and release it during peak periods, with the potential to significantly reduce power demand when it matters the most. Energy storage in buildings can be electrical or thermal, with thermal energy storage (TES) promising a more cost-effective solution than traditional electric batteries (Odukomaiya et al. 2021). Traditionally, TES systems have been used only for cooling or heating, but more recently, systems that can use TES with a high- performing HVAC system both for cooling and heating peaks have started being developed (U.S. Department of Energy 2024). • Develop advanced controls. This approach can be used with existing systems to precool/preheat the building to prevent spikes in demand during peak times (Xiong and Kim 2024). It can also be used in combination with new solutions to maximize their performance and capabilities. 2.3.2.3 Challenge Develop an innovative solution that will significantly reduce peak power demand in buildings. Students can focus on reducing thermal loads and improving HVAC systems. Teams should first develop a focused problem statement for a specific building type and location (weather region and power generation sources) and then develop a technical solution or process. Suggestions for student teams include (but are not limited to) the following: • Develop new cost-effective, high-efficiency systems that can replace or complement HVAC systems. • Develop technologies or processes that cost-effectively add energy storage to buildings. • Improve high-performance HVAC systems to maintain high efficiency during extreme cold days and reduce oversizing. • Develop a cost-effective combination of envelope improvements, energy storage, and advanced controls to minimize power consumption during peak periods. Of special interest are packaged solutions that combine hardware with advanced controls. 2.4 Technology Adoption Developing energy-efficient and cost-effective building technologies is only one side of the challenge. It is equally important to promote technology adoption so that solutions are accepted, integrated, and effectively used to improve energy management, building envelopes, and indoor environmental quality. 2.4.1 Solving Market Adoption for Emerging Efficiency Technologies 2.4.1.1 Objective Develop an innovative, holistic solution that will increase the purchase, installation, and use of energy-efficient technologies in buildings (residential, commercial, new, or existing).
